## Database search (DDA) {#sec-dda-search}

In data-dependent acquisition (DDA), peptide identification is typically performed by comparing experimental tandem mass spectra with theoretical spectra generated from a reference protein database [@McLafferty1981-xp; @Eng1994-bq; @Tyanova2016-rf]. Reference protein sequence databases are commonly obtained from UniProt [@UniProt-Consortium2018-vn]. The protein sequences are first digested *in silico* according to the same enzymatic rules used during sample preparation, producing a list of theoretical peptides. 
For each peptide, a theoretical fragmentation spectrum is generated by predicting the fragment ions expected during tandem mass spectrometry.

The experimental MS2 or MS/MS spectra are then compared against these theoretical spectra in a process known as database searching. Specialized search engines, including Andromeda [@Cox2011-mf] implemented in MaxQuant [@Cox2008-mo], SEQUEST [@Eng1994-bq], MSFragger [@Kong2017-mn], and MS-GF+ [@Kim2014-kw], evaluate how well each theoretical spectrum matches the observed experimental spectrum. Each comparison produces a peptide-spectrum match (PSM), which is assigned a score reflecting the quality of the match [@Sinitcyn2018-zo]. 
Although the underlying scoring algorithms differ between search engines, they all aim to distinguish correct peptide identifications from incorrect matches. 
For example, the Andromeda search engine uses a probabilistic scoring model to estimate the probability of observing a given match by chance (see @sec-andromeda-score) [@Cox2011-mf].

### Scoring algorithms

#### The Andromeda score {#sec-andromeda-score}

The Andromeda score algorithm [@Cox2011-mf], built into MaxQuant [@Cox2008-mo], scores peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) using a binomial probability model.
The score is based on how many theoretical fragment ions are matched in the experimental MS/MS spectrum, and is defined as the negative ten times the logarithm of the probability of observing at least that number of matches by chance.

## FDR calculation and statistical validation
Peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) are assigned scores that reflect how well an experimental spectrum matches a theoretical spectrum generated from a protein sequence database. Although these scores rank candidate peptide identifications, they do not directly indicate the probability that a match is correct. Consequently, an additional statistical framework is required to estimate the number of true and false peptide identifications.

The most widely used approach for estimating identification confidence is the target-decoy strategy, which provides an estimate of the false discovery rate (FDR) [@Elias2007-qh; @Benjamini1995-uj; @Storey2003-lq]. In this approach, a decoy database is generated alongside the target protein database, typically by reversing the protein sequences. The resulting decoy sequences preserve key properties of the target database, such as amino acid composition and sequence length, but do not correspond to real proteins. Consequently, any PSM assigned to a decoy sequence is considered a false positive.

The numbers of target and decoy identifications are then used to estimate the proportion of false positive identifications among the target matches. This estimation relies on the assumption that incorrect matches are equally likely to occur against the target and decoy databases [@Elias2007-qh]. By selecting a score threshold corresponding to a desired FDR, commonly 1%, researchers can control the expected proportion of false positive peptide identifications while retaining as many true identifications as possible.

The false discovery rate is defined as:

$$
\text{FDR} = \frac{\text{False Positives (FP)}}{\text{True Positives (TP)} + \text{False Positives (FP)}}
$$

In the context of the target-decoy approach, the number of false positive target hits is estimated by the number of decoy hits [@Moore2002-dz; @Granholm2012-az], so the formula becomes:

$$
\text{FDR} = \frac{\#\text{Decoy Hits}}{\#\text{Target Hits}}
$$

A commonly used implementation of the target-decoy approach is target-decoy competition (TDC), in which the experimental spectra are searched against a combined target-decoy database, and only the best match across all theoretical peptides (targets and decoys) is retained for each spectrum [@Peng2003-uk].

The MaxQuant computational platform additionally computes the posterior error probability (PEP), which is calculated using Bayes' theorem and reflects the quality of each PSM [@Tyanova2016-rf].
The PEP takes several peptide properties into account, such as peptide length, number of modifications, charge, and the search engine score.
The PEP is used to calculate the FDR at the PSM, peptide, protein, and PTM site level, ensuring correct estimation at all levels of identification [@Tyanova2016-rf].
Importantly, all scoring and filtering steps must be applied equally to target and decoy matches to ensure robust FDR estimation [@Cox2008-mo].

Machine learning (ML) methods used by some workflows to estimate the correctness of PSMs.
For example, Percolator uses a semi-supervised learning approach to distinguish correct from incorrect PSMs [@Kall2007-nm].
It trains a support vector machine (SVM) on features of both target and decoy matches, allowing for more accurate rescoring of PSMs and improved identification performance.
The input features are derived from the search engine output, such as the score, peptide length, and delta score (the difference between the best and the second-best score) [@Kall2007-nm].

## Protein inference

While peptide identification is relatively robust, translating peptide identifications back to the set of proteins from which they originated remains a complex computational challenge.
This is due to redundancy and shared sequence homology within the proteome, where many peptides map to multiple proteins and protein isoforms.
Protein inference must resolve which proteins are truly present in a sample based on the observed peptides, a task further complicated by incomplete sequence coverage.
Several approaches have been developed to address protein inference, and different inference strategies can yield different sets of reported proteins when starting from the same PSMs.
In MaxQuant, razor peptides (peptides that map to more than one protein) are assigned to the protein group with the most identified peptides.
Proteins that cannot be distinguished based on their identified peptides are reported together as a protein group [@Tyanova2016-rf].

## PTM analysis

### PTM identification 

Identification of post-translational modifications (PTMs) in mass spectrometry-based proteomics relies primarily on detecting mass shifts that correspond to the addition or removal of a specific chemical group on a modifiable amino acid residue [@Lennon1999-ki]. D
uring database searching, these expected mass shifts are incorporated into the search space, allowing modified peptide candidates to be matched to experimental spectra.

In addition to characteristic mass shifts, many PTMs produce diagnostic fragment ions or neutral losses during peptide fragmentation, providing additional evidence for modification assignment. 
For example, phosphorylated peptides may generate the phosphotyrosine-specific immonium ion at *m/z* = 216.042, which serves as a diagnostic reporter ion for phosphotyrosine-containing peptides [@Olsen2007-px]. 
Phosphorylated peptides can also undergo neutral loss of phosphoric acid during fragmentation, producing characteristic fragment ions that further support phosphorylation site identification [@Olsen2007-px]. 
These diagnostic ions and neutral loss patterns can be incorporated into the search space of database search engines to improve peptide identification [@Cox2011-mf]. 
For example, the Andromeda search engine explicitly evaluates spectra both with and without the expected neutral loss at the modification site and retains the higher of the two scores as the final peptide-spectrum match score [@Cox2011-mf].
